html:
SMTO-HTTP-0044 — SMTO couldn't confirm the service's security certificate

GUID: 29c1b18b-4305-4044-8eb0-604a43b96b38
Slug: http-tls-verification-failed
Domain: HTTP · Subsystem: http

What happened

  • The service couldn't prove its identity with a certificate SMTO trusts, so SMTO stopped before signing in or sending your request.

How to fix — simple steps

  1. Open Parameter Store, select the HTTP connection, and check that Base URL uses the service's full official name, not a short nickname or a numeric address. The certificate is issued for a specific name, and a different name fails the check.
  2. Ask the service's owner whether its certificate has expired or was issued by your organisation's own certificate authority. An expired certificate or a private issuer are the other common causes.
  3. For a private issuer, under TLS & transport set TLS verification to custom_ca and paste the issuer's certificate into CA certificate PEM, then save. This tells SMTO to trust your organisation's issuer without turning off the check.
  4. Select Test connection. When it shows Reachable, run the task again. The test confirms the certificate is now trusted.

What success looks like

  • Test connection shows Reachable while TLS verification is still system or custom_ca.

If it still fails

  • Select Copy error details and send them to whoever runs the service or your network. Don't set TLS verification to insecure or tick Allow unencrypted HTTP; the first removes the safety check and the second doesn't affect secure connections.

Technical details

Observed condition

  • The Gateway's TLS handshake failed certificate verification (hostname mismatch, expiry or an untrusted issuer; the specific defect is not identified).

What this means

  • The TLS layer reported certificate verification failure. A hostname mismatch, expiry or missing trusted issuer are different possible causes; the safe category does not identify which one occurred. Correct the certificate or trust chain for the intended host while keeping verification enabled.

Why this can happen

  • Certificate verification failed; the specific hostname, validity or issuer problem requires certificate inspection.

How to diagnose it

  • Have the service or network administrator inspect the certificate for the configured hostname, its validity dates and issuer chain. If a private CA is intended, verify that CA through a trusted channel before configuring custom_ca.

How to fix it

  • Inspect the presented chain from the Gateway host (for example openssl s_client -connect with -servername), then repair the server certificate or chain, or set the profile's TLS verification to custom_ca with the trusted private CA. Keep verification enabled; allow_insecure_http controls plain HTTP only.
  • Repair the certificate chain or use custom_ca with the trusted private CA. Never automatically weaken verification. allow_insecure_http controls plain HTTP only.

Retry and execution caution

  • Apply the correction and confirm the relevant state before requesting another attempt. Prior completed work remains governed by its receipts.

How to verify the fix

  • Verify the HTTPS connection succeeds with the intended hostname and trusted chain while certificate verification stays enabled.

What not to do

  • Do not set allow_insecure_http to repair HTTPS certificate verification.
  • Do not disable certificate verification or accept an unverified certificate as the default fix.

Technical notes

  • Standard certificate-verification markers classify the TLS failure; the exact certificate defect is not established.
  • Preserve the occurrence ID and safe request/operation references. Receipts and occurrence facts establish what started or completed; the catalog does not authorize retries or establish execution outcome.

Do not confuse with / related errors
